About this simulation

On screen
One plot against n. Thin stems of height 1/n with a small dot on top, solid dots at the partial sums SN of 1/n, and open blue circles at the partial sums TN of 1/n2, each at n = N. Linear view: n from 0 to 21, heights 0 to 4. Logarithmic view: n from 1 to 1000, heights 0 to 8. A dashed line at π²/6 appears once N reaches 100. Grouped view (the notes' Figure 2, unlocked after card 4 in the guided inquiry): bars of height 1/n for n = 1 to 16, heights 0 to 1, with a shaded lower bound in each bar (the last term of its group), brackets over n = 3–4, 5–8 and 9–16 marked sum ≥ 1/2, and the bound S2k ≥ 1 + k/2 of eq. (1.10) listed at the right.
Controls
Number of terms N (1 to 20 on the linear axis, 1 to 1000 on the logarithmic one). Step adds one term, Reset returns N to 1, Play adds two terms per second on the linear axis and advances evenly along the logarithmic axis. The n axis switch chooses the view; switching to linear with N above 20 sets N to 20, and switching to grouped sets N to 16 (Step and Play then rebuild it from N = 1).
Measured
1/N, 1/N2, SN and TN come straight from the engine's partial sums; the dashed line is ζ(2) = π²/6 from the engine's zeta function.

Guided Inquiry

1 · One more term

The n axis is linear and N is 5. Before pressing Step +1 term to add the sixth term, predict how far the new black dot at n = 6 will sit above the black dot at n = 5. Then press Step +1 term and compare the two values of SN in the readout.

2 · The sums of 1/n²

The n axis is linear and N is back at 1. You will press Play in the header and let N run to 20. Before pressing Play, predict what the blue circles, the partial sums of 1/n2, will do.

3 · The sums of 1/n, up to 1000

N is at 20 and the n axis is now the logarithmic one. You will press Play and let N run to 1000, which takes about 20 s (10 s at 2× speed). Before pressing Play, predict how the black dots, the partial sums of 1/n, will look on this axis.

4 · Five hundred tiny terms

The axis is logarithmic and N is 500; note SN in the readout. You will then set N to 1000. Before doing so, predict how much SN will grow over these 500 further terms, each smaller than 0.002.

5 · What the two series show

The axis is logarithmic with N at 1000, where the latest terms in the readout are 1/N = 0.001 and 1/N2 = 0.000001. Before switching back to the linear axis to look at the stems once more, decide which statement about series the two sets of dots support.

6 · Terms tending to zero are not enough

For a series to converge its terms must tend to zero, since uN = SN − SN−1. The converse is false. The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ⋯ has terms tending to zero, yet each doubling of N adds at least ½, so SN ≈ ln N + 0.577 grows without limit. The grouped (Fig. 2) setting of the n axis draws this argument: S2k ≥ 1 + k/2.

The terms 1/n2 fall fast enough: the sums TN settle at π2/6 = 1.6449, the dashed line. What decides convergence is how fast the terms fall: Σ 1/np converges for p > 1 and diverges for p ≤ 1.

The Physics

Adding Up Smaller and Smaller Terms · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Two series are added one term at a time: the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ and the series of squares 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ⋯. The sim draws each term as a stem against n and marks the running totals, the partial sums, with dots and circles.

What you'll learn

  • What a partial sum is and how it is built from the terms.
  • How the partial sums of the two series behave as N grows.
  • What decides whether a sum of ever smaller terms is finite.
The sim's plot, drawn schematically at N = 4 on the linear axis. Each n carries a stem, a black dot and a blue circle.

What's on screen

  • Stems: a thin line of height 1/n, topped by a small dot, at each n from 1 to N.
  • Black dots and blue circles: the partial sums SN of 1/n and TN of 1/n², at each n.
  • Readouts: N, the latest terms 1/N and 1/N², and the partial sums SN = Σ 1/n and TN = Σ 1/n².
See itLook at the sim as it opens. Watch for: a single stem of height 1 with the black dot and the blue circle on its top.

03

The partial sums SN and TN add the first N terms of 1/n and of 1/n²

Both series come from one list of terms: un = 1/n for the harmonic series and un = 1/n² for the series of squares. The N-th partial sum adds the first N terms (notes, eq. 1.7):

SN = ∑n=1N 1/n    TN = ∑n=1N 1/n²
The partial sums the sim plots.

A series converges to a sum when its partial sums tend to a limit, and diverges otherwise. The sim draws SN as a black dot and TN as a blue circle above n = N, with a stem of height 1/n at every n.

Both series start with the term 1, so at N = 1 the stem, the dot and the circle all sit at height 1. For every larger N there are two partial sums to read at once. They are what the lower readouts report: for N = 3, S3 = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 = 1.8333 and T3 = 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 = 1.3611.

Key idea. A partial sum is a running total, and each N gives one value of it.
See itSet N = 3 on the linear axis. Watch for: three stems of heights 1, 1/2 and 1/3, with the dot at 1.8333 and the circle at 1.3611.
04

Each new term lifts the partial sum by exactly its own height

Going from N − 1 to N adds one term to each sum (eq. 1.7), so:

SN − SN−1 = 1/N    TN − TN−1 = 1/N²
Each climb is the new term.

Every climb of a black dot is therefore exactly the height of the new stem. From S5 = 2.2833 to S6 = 2.4500 the climb is 0.1667 = 1/6, the stem at n = 6. The blue circles climb by the squares of the stems: T6 − T5 = 1/36 = 0.0278.

S5 to S6 and the new stem, on the same vertical scale. The two lengths are equal.
Key idea. The size of each step is the size of the term just added, 1/N here.
See itSet N = 5 and read SN. Watch for: the black dot at 2.2833 and the newest stem of height 0.2.
See itPress Step +1 term once, to N = 6. Watch for: SN rising to 2.4500, an increase of 0.1667.
05

The squares level off just below π²/6, because TN stays under 2

The comparison test (notes, eq. 1.11) bounds TN. Since n + 1 ≤ 2n,

1/n² ≤ 2/[n(n + 1)] = 2(1/n − 1/(n + 1))
The comparison behind the blue circles.

Adding from n = 1 to N, the −1/(n + 1) of each bracket cancels the 1/(n + 1) of the next, so TN ≤ 2[1 − 1/(N + 1)] < 2. The partial sums never decrease and never exceed 2, so they tend to a limit, which is at most 2.

The blue circles for n up to 20, under the bound and the dashed line.

The sim marks the limit, π²/6 = 1.6449, with a dashed line once N reaches 100. The notes obtain π²/6 later, from a Fourier series. At N = 20, T20 = 1.5962; at N = 100, T100 = 1.6350. The gap to π²/6 is close to 1/N, 0.0100 at N = 100, so it shrinks in step with the terms.

Key idea. TN rises at every step but cannot pass 2, so it settles on a limit, here π²/6 = 1.6449.
See itPress ▶ Play on the linear axis, or look at N = 20. Watch for: the blue circles flattening out near 1.6 while the black dots keep rising.
See itSwitch to the log axis with N = 100. Watch for: the dashed π²/6 line appearing, with TN just below it at 1.6350.
06

The harmonic sums climb along a straight line on the log axis, 2.3 for each factor of 10

The black dots do not level off. On the log axis they lie on a straight line, SN ≈ ln N + 0.577. A factor of 10 in N adds ln 10 = 2.30: S10 = 2.93, S100 = 5.19 and S1000 = 7.49, steps of 2.26 and 2.30.

The partial sums of 1/n against a log axis for N. The dashed line is ln N + 0.577.

The constant 0.577 is Euler's constant. It is a standard result that the notes do not derive. At N = 1000 the formula gives 7.4850 and the sim 7.4855. A straight line against ln N is slow growth but growth without limit: SN passes 10 only at N = 12,367, and by this formula it passes 100 only near N = 1043.

N

This slider moves the sim's N too, on a log scale from 1 to 1000. Above 20 it switches the sim to the log axis.

Key idea. Each factor of 10 in N adds the same 2.3 to SN, so it never settles.
See itGo to N = 10 on the log axis. Watch for: the black dot at 2.9290.
See itThen N = 100. Watch for: SN at 5.1874, 2.26 higher.
See itThen N = 1000. Watch for: SN at 7.4855, 2.30 higher, with the dots on a straight line.
07

Every doubling of N adds at least 1/2, so the harmonic sum has no limit

The notes prove it by grouping the terms (eq. 1.9): keep 1 and 1/2, then bracket 1/3 + 1/4, then 1/5 + ⋯ + 1/8, then 1/9 + ⋯ + 1/16, and so on. The bracket that ends at 1/2k holds 2k−1 terms, each at least 1/2k, so it adds at least 1/2.

The notes' Figure 2. Every group adds to at least 1/2, shown by the shaded lower bounds.

Counting the first two terms and k − 1 brackets gives S2k ≥ 1 + k/2 (eq. 1.10), which exceeds any number once k is large. So S16 = 3.3807 is above 3, and S1024 = 7.5092 is above 6.

The true gain per doubling is about ln 2 = 0.69. The 500 terms from N = 500 to N = 1000 are each less than 0.002, yet together they add 0.69, from S500 = 6.7928 to S1000 = 7.4855.

Key idea. Many tiny terms add up: every doubling of N adds at least 1/2, and in fact about 0.69.
See itGo to N = 500 on the log axis and note SN, then to N = 1000. Watch for: SN growing by about 0.69, from 6.7928 to 7.4855.
See itSwitch the n axis to grouped. Watch for: the three brackets marked sum ≥ 1/2 and the sim's line S16 = 3.381 ≥ 3.
08

Terms tending to zero are necessary for a finite sum, but not sufficient

If a series converges, its terms must tend to zero, because uN = SN − SN−1 and both partial sums tend to the same limit (notes, §1.1). The converse is false, and the harmonic series is the notes' example.

At N = 1000 the latest terms are 1/N = 0.001 and 1/N² = 0.000001, both tiny. Yet SN has reached 7.4855 and is still climbing, while TN has stopped at about 1.644.

What decides the matter is how fast the terms fall. The terms 1/n fall too slowly, since every doubling adds at least 1/2. The terms 1/n² fall fast enough, since they stay below 2/[n(n + 1)] and the sum cancels itself. The notes give a further comparison: since 1/√n ≥ 1/n, the series ∑ 1/√n diverges too.

Key idea. Terms that shrink to zero are needed for a finite sum, but how fast they shrink decides it.
See itSet N = 1000 on the log axis and read the first three readouts. Watch for: 1/N = 0.001 beside SN = 7.4855.
09

Summary

In one line. The sim adds the terms 1/n and 1/n² one at a time and plots the running totals, SN and TN, against the number of terms N.
  • SN − SN−1 = 1/N: each climb is the height of the new stem.
  • TN ≤ 2[1 − 1/(N + 1)], and it levels off at π²/6 = 1.6449.
  • SN ≈ ln N + 0.577 and S2k ≥ 1 + k/2: no limit.
  • Terms tending to zero are necessary for a finite sum, not sufficient.

Common mix-ups

  • "The terms go to zero, so the sum is finite." At N = 1000, 1/N = 0.001 and SN = 7.4855 is still rising.
  • "A sum that always rises has no limit." TN rises at every step and stays below π²/6.
  • "The black dots are levelling off." Only on the linear axis; on the log axis they climb 2.3 per factor of 10.

Things to try on your own

  • Press Step from N = 1: S4 = 2.0833 passes the bound 1 + 2/2 = 2.
